screens.title: BGP Message Types and Neighbor States
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we explore the messages that make BGP work and the Finite State Machine that governs neighbor sessions. You will learn what information appears in the Open message that starts a session, why Update messages are the workhorse for exchanging reachability, how Keepalive messages act as a heartbeat, and when Notification messages tear a session down. We will also map these messages to the six FSM neighbor states — Idle, Connect, Active, OpenSent, OpenConfirm, and Established — and show how state transitions reveal common configuration and connectivity problems. Understanding this mapping is essential for both setting up peerings and for focused troubleshooting: a session stuck in Active points you to TCP connectivity, whereas an OpenSent hang often means a parameter mismatch. By the end of the chapter you should be able to read neighbor states, interpret message types, and follow a simple troubleshooting checklist to isolate firewall, routing, or configuration issues. Consider a two-router lab where bring-up moves from Open to Established — that practical scenario will ground the concepts and help you predict failures.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives lay out the practical skills you'll gain. First, you'll identify and describe the four primary BGP message types and their functions, so you can read a packet capture or log and understand whether a peer is opening a session, advertising routes, sending a heartbeat, or throwing an error. Second, you'll explain the purpose of the BGP Finite State Machine and how it governs session establishment and teardown, which helps you reason about why peers stop or fail. Third, you'll detail transitions between the six neighbor states — Idle, Connect, Active, OpenSent, OpenConfirm, and Established — so you can map symptoms to likely causes. Finally, you'll recognize common causes of BGP session failures from observed neighbor states and know a focused initial troubleshooting checklist. Each objective ties to practical checks you can run on a Junos device and to decisions you'll make when fixing peering issues in a lab or production network.

screens.title: The Four BGP Message Types
screens.narratorSegment: BGP uses four fundamental message types to manage sessions and exchange routing information. First, the Open message is the session initiator. It announces the BGP version, the sender's Autonomous System number, the negotiated hold time, and the router identifier. Optional parameters, like authentication, may also appear. If required parameters do not match between peers, the Open exchange will fail and a Notification is produced. Second, Update messages are the workhorse: they carry NLRI — the prefixes being advertised or withdrawn — and include path attributes like AS path and next hop. Updates tell a peer which networks are reachable and how to reach them. Third, Keepalive messages are periodic, small-hearted confirmations sent at intervals to show the peer is still responsive; they are typically sent at one third of the negotiated hold time. If neither a Keepalive nor an Update arrives before the hold time expires, the session is considered down and routes are withdrawn. Fourth, Notification messages signal fatal errors and immediately tear the session down; they include an error code and subcode explaining the reason. A common misconception is to treat Notification as a regular alarm; in reality it always indicates a protocol-level or configuration error that needs correction before reestablishing the session. As a takeaway, remember: Open to agree parameters, Update to exchange reachability, Keepalive to maintain the liveness, Notification to report fatal errors.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Message Types
The Four BGP Message Types
Open, Update, Keepalive, Notification — each with a clear operational role.
Definition and role
  • Open: Announces BGP version, AS, hold time, and Router ID. Peers must agree on parameters.
  • Update: Advertises or withdraws NLRI and includes path attributes that affect routing decisions.
  • Keepalive: Lightweight heartbeat sent regularly to confirm liveness.
  • Notification: Sent on error with a code and subcode; it immediately ends the session.
Common misconception: a Notification is not a benign warning — it always causes session termination.
Concrete example
Two routers begin peering. They exchange Open messages to agree on hold time and AS numbers. After Open and Keepalive, they exchange Update messages advertising prefixes. If one router sends an Update with an invalid format, the other responds with Notification and closes the session.
Key takeaway
Key Takeaway

Each message type has a single operational purpose; mapping messages to state behavior is the foundation of targeted troubleshooting.

screens.title: Open Message Contents and Failures
screens.narratorSegment: The Open message is the very first protocol-level exchange between BGP peers and carries the parameters that determine whether a session can proceed. It includes the BGP version, the sender's Autonomous System number, the negotiated hold time, and the BGP Router ID. Optional parameters may include authentication data. For a session to progress, certain parameters must match or be acceptable to both sides. For example, a mismatched AS number in the Open message will usually trigger a Notification and immediate session closure. Another common source of failure is an incompatible hold time or unsupported optional parameters. An OpenSent state that never reaches OpenConfirm often signals one peer is not receiving the other's Open — possibly due to one-way connectivity or an interfering middlebox. A useful troubleshooting thought process starts with checking TCP reachability to port 179 and confirming the configured neighbor AS and peer IP. A concrete lab scenario is changing the configured peer AS on one router and observing the Notification and session reset on both sides. The key misconception is assuming Open only announces identity; it actually negotiates session behavior and enforces compatibility, so mismatches will prevent any route exchange until corrected.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Open Message
Open Message Contents and Failures
What Open negotiates and how to detect mismatches.
Open message fields
  • Version: BGP protocol version number.
  • Autonomous System number: The sender's AS used for external and internal peering decisions.
  • Hold time: Maximum interval to wait for Keepalive or Update before declaring peer down.
  • Router ID: An IP used to uniquely identify the speaker.
If these do not align, a Notification is sent and the session closes.
Concrete troubleshooting example
Change the configured peer AS on one router. The local router sends an Open with the wrong AS. The remote router detects the mismatch and replies with a Notification. Both neighbors reset the session.
Quick checks
  • Verify neighbor IP and AS configuration matches the peer.
  • Confirm TCP connectivity to port 179 and interface status.
  • Look for asymmetric routing or one-way communication preventing Open delivery.

screens.title: Update Messages and NLRI
screens.narratorSegment: Update messages are the mechanism BGP uses to communicate reachability information between peers. Each Update can advertise new prefixes, withdraw previously advertised prefixes, or change attributes on existing routes. The advertised information includes NLRI — the network layer reachability information, which is the prefix itself — plus path attributes such as the AS path and next hop. While we will study attributes in detail later, for troubleshooting it is sufficient to know that updates carry both what networks exist and metadata that influences route selection. A concrete example: when a router advertises 192.0.2.0/24 with a next hop and AS path, the receiving peer adds that NLRI to its BGP table and may propagate it to its local routing table depending on preference. A common misconception is assuming Update messages are always large; in quiet networks they are small, while in large churn they can become frequent and cause instability. Understanding Update behavior helps explain why an Established session is desirable — only in that state do peers exchange Updates and thus actual routing information. The takeaway is to watch Update frequency and content when diagnosing route visibility problems or unexpected withdrawals.

keyIdea.title: Update role
keyIdea.text: Updates advertise and withdraw NLRI with path attributes; they determine which routes enter the BGP and forwarding tables.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Update Messages
Update Messages and NLRI
How route advertisements and withdrawals change reachability.
What an Update contains
  • NLRI: The prefixes being announced or withdrawn.
  • Path attributes: Metadata such as AS path and next hop that influence selection.
  • Withdrawals: Indicate previously advertised prefixes are no longer reachable.
Updates shape what routes are accepted into the BGP table and potentially into the routing table.
Concrete example
Router A advertises 203.0.113.0/24 with a next hop and AS path. Router B receives the Update and records the NLRI and attributes. If later Router A withdraws that prefix, Router B removes it from its BGP table and withdraws dependent forwarding state.
Key takeaway
Key Takeaway

Watch Update content and frequency: they directly control which prefixes are visible and when they are removed.

screens.title: Keepalive Messages and the Hold Timer
screens.narratorSegment: Keepalive messages are the simple heartbeat that tells a peer the session is still alive. After two peers complete the Open exchange and reach OpenConfirm, they send Keepalive messages at regular intervals to ensure the other side remains responsive. The interval is typically one third of the negotiated hold time, which is itself chosen during the Open exchange. If a router fails to receive either a Keepalive or an Update within the hold time, it assumes the peer is down and tears down the session, withdrawing routes learned from that neighbor. Practically, this means the hold timer is your detection window: a shorter hold time detects failures faster but may lead to more frequent resets in marginal networks; a longer hold time tolerates transient problems but delays detection. A common misconception is to expect Keepalives to be large — they are small and periodic. For troubleshooting, if routes disappear suddenly check whether the peer hit a hold-time expiry, which could result from lost Keepalives due to packet loss, overloaded C P U on the peer, or asymmetric routing preventing Keepalive delivery. Use the hold-time behavior to reason about how quickly a session will fail and what transient conditions are likely suspects.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Keepalive & Hold Timer
Keepalive Messages and the Hold Timer
Heartbeat behavior, timing, and failure consequences.
Process steps
1. After Open exchange, peers send Keepalives to confirm the session.
2. Keepalives are typically sent every one-third of the negotiated hold time.
3. If no Keepalive or Update arrives before the hold expires, the session is declared down and routes are withdrawn.
Concrete example
If peers negotiate a 90-second hold time, they will exchange Keepalives roughly every 30 seconds. If one peer stops receiving those messages for 90 seconds, it tears down the session and withdraws learned prefixes.
Troubleshooting tip
When routes vanish unexpectedly, check for hold-time expiry, packet loss, CPU exhaustion on the peer, or asymmetric routing preventing Keepalive delivery.

screens.title: Notification Messages and Error Handling
screens.narratorSegment: Notification messages are the protocol's way of saying a fatal error has occurred and the session cannot continue. They carry an error code and subcode that indicate the reason for termination — for example, an incorrect AS in the Open, an invalid Update, or a hold timer expiration. When a Notification is received, the affected session is immediately torn down. This is deliberate: continuing after a protocol-level error could lead to incorrect routing information being accepted. A typical example from the chapter is an AS mismatch during Open; the receiver sends a Notification and both peers reset the session. It is a common mistake to treat Notification as a transient log message. In practice, receipt of a Notification requires corrective action: review the error code, fix the configuration or software bug, and then reestablish the session. When troubleshooting, capture the Notification information where available; this will point directly to the offending field — whether a mismatched AS, malformed Update, or expired timer — and avoids blind guessing. The closing lesson: Notifications stop the session to protect routing correctness, and they should guide immediate corrective steps.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Notification
Notification Messages and Error Handling
How notifications force a session reset and what to do next.
What to expect
  • Notifications contain an error code and subcode with a clear reason for session termination.
  • They are triggered by protocol-level errors such as malformed Updates, AS mismatches, or hold-time expiry.
  • Receipt of Notification always ends the session immediately.
Concrete corrective steps
When you see a Notification, capture the code, inspect the Open and Update exchanges, and fix the offending configuration or implementation error before reestablishing the peering.
Key takeaway
A Notification is not a passive warning. It is a deliberate protocol response requiring a fix.

screens.title: BGP Finite State Machine (FSM)
screens.narratorSegment: The BGP Finite State Machine organizes the steps for establishing and maintaining a peering session. It defines six neighbor states: Idle, Connect, Active, OpenSent, OpenConfirm, and Established. Idle is the starting point where the process is not attempting to form a session. When the speaker initiates a TCP connection the FSM moves to Connect; a succeeding TCP handshake sends the FSM to OpenSent, where the local side has sent an Open and awaits the peer's Open. If the TCP connection cannot be created, the FSM moves to Active and keeps trying — a signal that TCP connectivity or routing to the peer is failing. Upon receiving a peer Open, a speaker enters OpenConfirm and exchanges Keepalive to confirm the parameters. Finally, after successful Keepalive exchange the session reaches Established and Update messages flow. Transitions are driven by concrete events: successful TCP connection, receipt of specific messages, or timeouts. A practical misconception is to treat Active as a BGP problem; it almost always points to TCP connectivity issues like blocked port 179, incorrect peer IP, or routing problems. Understanding this sequence allows you to map observed state to a short list of focused checks and avoid wasted effort on irrelevant settings.

keyIdea.text: Each FSM state corresponds to a specific step or problem domain — use the state to guide whether to check TCP, parameters, or keepalive timing.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › FSM Overview
BGP Finite State Machine (FSM)
Six neighbor states and the events that drive transitions.
State list and intent
  • Idle: Not attempting; waiting for a start event.
  • Connect: Initiating TCP connection to peer.
  • Active: Trying to establish TCP; often indicates connectivity issues.
  • OpenSent: TCP established and Open sent, awaiting peer Open.
  • OpenConfirm: Open received and Keepalive exchanged, awaiting confirmation.
  • Established: Session fully operational and exchanging Updates.
Concrete example
When you start peering, logs will show transition from Idle to Connect to OpenSent to OpenConfirm and finally to Established if all TCP and parameter checks succeed. A transition to Active suggests you need to check reachability and port 179 filtering first.
Key takeaway
Read the neighbor state first to narrow the cause: connectivity, parameter mismatch, or normal operation.

screens.title: Idle and Connect States — Entry and Failure Modes
screens.narratorSegment: Idle is the entry state for BGP. A speaker in Idle is not attempting to form a session; it may be administratively disabled or waiting for a start event. If you see Idle persistently, first check whether the BGP process or the neighbor statement is active. Moving from Idle to Connect happens when the speaker initiates a TCP connection to its peer. Connect indicates the system has started active connection attempts. If the TCP handshake succeeds the state moves to OpenSent. If the TCP handshake fails, the FSM moves to Active and repeatedly attempts a connection. Common root causes for a failed Connect include incorrect local configuration that prevents the start event, misconfigured neighbor IP, or a local interface being down. Practically, check that the neighbor is enabled, the interface addressing is correct, and that there is an IP route to the peer before concluding the problem is deeper. A frequent misconception is to assume Idle implies a remote problem; often the local router is not configured to initiate peering or the BGP group is deactivated. Confirm both sides are configured and that TCP can be established to proceed.

keyIdea.title: Start-up checks
keyIdea.text: Idle means no start; Connect means TCP attempted — verify local BGP configuration, interface state, and reachability before blaming the peer.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Idle & Connect
Idle and Connect States — Entry and Failure Modes
When peering hasn't started or when TCP connection is being attempted.
Idle state checks
  • Is the BGP group or neighbor administratively active?
  • Are the local interfaces and addresses configured and up?
  • Has the routing table an entry to reach the peer?
Connect troubleshooting
If the router cannot complete the TCP handshake, verify peer IPs, check for firewall rules blocking port 179, and ensure there is no asymmetric routing that prevents TCP completion.

screens.title: Active and OpenSent — Connectivity vs Parameter Problems
screens.narratorSegment: Active and OpenSent are neighboring states that point to different root causes. Active means the speaker is still trying to establish a TCP connection to its peer; it repeatedly attempts new TCP connections. This almost always indicates a connectivity issue, such as a firewall blocking TCP port 179, an incorrect neighbor IP, or a routing problem preventing reachability. Your initial checks should be ping tests, interface status checks, and firewall rule inspection. In contrast, OpenSent means the TCP connection was successful and the local speaker has sent its Open message; it is now waiting for the peer's Open. If OpenSent persists without progressing, it suggests a parameter mismatch or a one-way communication issue where the peer's Open never arrives. Common mismatches include wrong AS numbers or authentication parameters. A practical troubleshooting sequence is to confirm TCP succeeds first, then verify the Open fields match (AS, hold time, Router ID expectations). A common misconception is to skip the TCP check and jump into BGP settings. Always verify the network pipe before diagnosing protocol parameters. Ending question to consider: if you can TCP to port 179 but remain in OpenSent, what Open field would you inspect first?

Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Active & OpenSent
Active and OpenSent — Connectivity vs Parameter Problems
Use simple checks to quickly isolate the problem domain.
Active troubleshooting checklist
  1. Ping the peer IP to confirm basic reachability.
  2. Confirm no firewall or ACL blocks TCP port 179.
  3. Check interface and route status to the peer.
OpenSent checks
If TCP completes but OpenSent persists, verify the configured neighbor AS and any authentication parameters. Also consider packet capture to confirm the peer's Open arrives.

screens.title: OpenConfirm and Established — Confirmation and Route Exchange
screens.narratorSegment: OpenConfirm and Established are the final stages of the FSM. OpenConfirm occurs after a peer's Open is received and the local speaker has sent a Keepalive. It is a short state where the speakers confirm they have agreed on parameters. If both sides exchange Keepalive successfully, the session moves to Established. Established is the desired operational state: both peers have completed the handshake and now exchange Update messages containing NLRI and attributes. This is where routing information flows and the network becomes aware of offered prefixes. A frequent misconception is to interpret Established as a guarantee that all routing policies are correct — it only guarantees that the session is operational and Update exchange will occur. You still need to verify that the advertised NLRI and path attributes reflect the intended policy. For monitoring and troubleshooting, reaching Established means you can inspect Update contents to resolve prefix visibility issues. The closing question to apply: when in Established, which message type will you inspect to determine why a prefix is missing from a peer? content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › OpenConfirm & Established
OpenConfirm and Established — Confirmation and Route Exchange
What confirmation looks like and why Established matters.
OpenConfirm role
After Open reception, peers exchange Keepalives to confirm negotiated parameters. Successful exchange moves the FSM to Established.
Established behavior
Peers exchange Update messages and the network learns advertised prefixes. Policies and attributes still determine which routes are accepted into the routing table.
Key takeaway
Established confirms peer compatibility and connectivity but does not guarantee policy alignment or desired route selection.

screens.title: Lab Walkthrough: Junos eBGP Peering and State Observation
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on walkthrough uses a simple two-router Junos configuration to bring up an eBGP peering and observe state changes. The chapter provides base configuration for R1 (AS 65001) and R2 (AS 65002) with a /30 point-to-point link. Start by applying the snippet on both routers and commit. On R1 run show bgp summary and show bgp neighbor to watch the neighbor move from Idle through OpenSent, OpenConfirm, to Established. To simulate faults, deactivate the BGP group on R1 and observe R2 move out of Established. Next, intentionally change R1's neighbor peer-as to an incorrect AS and commit; you should see the session fail and Notification messages indicating an AS mismatch. Practical checks to run when a session is stuck in Active are ping to the peer, verify interface status, and ensure port 179 is not blocked. When a session stalls in OpenSent, compare configured AS numbers and authentication parameters. The configuration snippet below is the exact text to use in the lab. Follow the sequence: commit base config, observe transition to Established, deactivate the group and observe withdrawal, then re-activate, change peer-as to trigger Notification, and revert.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Lab Walkthrough
Lab Walkthrough: Junos eBGP Peering and State Observation

R1 configuration (AS 65001)

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 1
screens.narratorSegment: These key concepts summarize the chapter's most important operational points. First, Open messages negotiate the session parameters — version, AS, hold time, and Router ID — and mismatches here produce Notifications that terminate the session. Second, Update messages are how routers exchange NLRI and path attributes; they directly determine which prefixes are visible to peers and which enter the routing table. Third, Keepalive messages are the heartbeat mechanism sent at roughly one third of the negotiated hold time; failure to receive Keepalive or Update before the hold timer expires causes the session to be considered down. Keep these three ideas in mind when reading logs or capturing packets: they tell you whether a problem is negotiation, reachability, or liveness related. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we explore the messages that make BGP work and the Finite State Machine that governs neighbor sessions. You will learn what information appears in the Open message that starts a session, why Update messages are the workhorse for exchanging reachability, how Keepalive messages act as a heartbeat, and when Notification messages tear a session down. We will also map these messages to the six FSM neighbor states — Idle, Connect, Active, OpenSent, OpenConfirm, and Established — and show how state transitions reveal common configuration and connectivity problems. Understanding this mapping is essential for both setting up peerings and for focused troubleshooting: a session stuck in Active points you to TCP connectivity, whereas an OpenSent hang often means a parameter mismatch. By the end of the chapter you should be able to read neighbor states, interpret message types, and follow a simple troubleshooting checklist to isolate firewall, routing, or configuration issues. Consider a two-router lab where bring-up moves from Open to Established — that practical scenario will ground the concepts and help you predict failures.

These objectives lay out the practical skills you'll gain. First, you'll identify and describe the four primary BGP message types and their functions, so you can read a packet capture or log and understand whether a peer is opening a session, advertising routes, sending a heartbeat, or throwing an error. Second, you'll explain the purpose of the BGP Finite State Machine and how it governs session establishment and teardown, which helps you reason about why peers stop or fail. Third, you'll detail transitions between the six neighbor states — Idle, Connect, Active, OpenSent, OpenConfirm, and Established — so you can map symptoms to likely causes. Finally, you'll recognize common causes of BGP session failures from observed neighbor states and know a focused initial troubleshooting checklist. Each objective ties to practical checks you can run on a Junos device and to decisions you'll make when fixing peering issues in a lab or production network.

These additional objectives focus on practical application and troubleshooting. You will interpret neighbor state output and decide the most efficient next check, such as ping for reachability or show commands for configuration errors. You will practice reading Update messages conceptually to know what network reachability information and path attributes are being exchanged, even without decoding every attribute immediately. And you will simulate bring-up and deliberate misconfiguration in a lab to see how states move and how Notification messages arise from parameter mismatches. These activities reinforce the conceptual model and make troubleshooting muscle-memory: when you see Active, you expect a TCP problem; when you see OpenSent that never completes, you suspect AS or authentication mismatch. This mental mapping reduces guesswork and speeds restoration in real networks. Learning Objectives — Continued means translate state observations into targeted checks: reachability, interface status, firewall rules, and configuration alignment.. In practical terms, skills you will practice and checks to master. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

BGP uses four fundamental message types to manage sessions and exchange routing information. First, the Open message is the session initiator. It announces the BGP version, the sender's Autonomous System number, the negotiated hold time, and the router identifier. Optional parameters, like authentication, may also appear. If required parameters do not match between peers, the Open exchange will fail and a Notification is produced. Second, Update messages are the workhorse: they carry NLRI — the prefixes being advertised or withdrawn — and include path attributes like AS path and next hop. Updates tell a peer which networks are reachable and how to reach them. Third, Keepalive messages are periodic, small-hearted confirmations sent at intervals to show the peer is still responsive; they are typically sent at one third of the negotiated hold time. If neither a Keepalive nor an Update arrives before the hold time expires, the session is considered down and routes are withdrawn. Fourth, Notification messages signal fatal errors and immediately tear the session down; they include an error code and subcode explaining the reason. A common misconception is to treat Notification as a regular alarm; in reality it always indicates a protocol-level or configuration error that needs correction before reestablishing the session. As a takeaway, remember: Open to agree parameters, Update to exchange reachability, Keepalive to maintain the liveness, Notification to report fatal errors.

The Open message is the very first protocol-level exchange between BGP peers and carries the parameters that determine whether a session can proceed. It includes the BGP version, the sender's Autonomous System number, the negotiated hold time, and the BGP Router ID. Optional parameters may include authentication data. For a session to progress, certain parameters must match or be acceptable to both sides. For example, a mismatched AS number in the Open message will usually trigger a Notification and immediate session closure. Another common source of failure is an incompatible hold time or unsupported optional parameters. An OpenSent state that never reaches OpenConfirm often signals one peer is not receiving the other's Open — possibly due to one-way connectivity or an interfering middlebox. A useful troubleshooting thought process starts with checking TCP reachability to port 179 and confirming the configured neighbor AS and peer IP. A concrete lab scenario is changing the configured peer AS on one router and observing the Notification and session reset on both sides. The key misconception is assuming Open only announces identity; it actually negotiates session behavior and enforces compatibility, so mismatches will prevent any route exchange until corrected.

Update messages are the mechanism BGP uses to communicate reachability information between peers. Each Update can advertise new prefixes, withdraw previously advertised prefixes, or change attributes on existing routes. The advertised information includes NLRI — the network layer reachability information, which is the prefix itself — plus path attributes such as the AS path and next hop. While we will study attributes in detail later, for troubleshooting it is sufficient to know that updates carry both what networks exist and metadata that influences route selection. A concrete example: when a router advertises 192.0.2.0/24 with a next hop and AS path, the receiving peer adds that NLRI to its BGP table and may propagate it to its local routing table depending on preference. A common misconception is assuming Update messages are always large; in quiet networks they are small, while in large churn they can become frequent and cause instability. Understanding Update behavior helps explain why an Established session is desirable — only in that state do peers exchange Updates and thus actual routing information. The takeaway is to watch Update frequency and content when diagnosing route visibility problems or unexpected withdrawals.

Keepalive messages are the simple heartbeat that tells a peer the session is still alive. After two peers complete the Open exchange and reach OpenConfirm, they send Keepalive messages at regular intervals to ensure the other side remains responsive. The interval is typically one third of the negotiated hold time, which is itself chosen during the Open exchange. If a router fails to receive either a Keepalive or an Update within the hold time, it assumes the peer is down and tears down the session, withdrawing routes learned from that neighbor. Practically, this means the hold timer is your detection window: a shorter hold time detects failures faster but may lead to more frequent resets in marginal networks; a longer hold time tolerates transient problems but delays detection. A common misconception is to expect Keepalives to be large — they are small and periodic. For troubleshooting, if routes disappear suddenly check whether the peer hit a hold-time expiry, which could result from lost Keepalives due to packet loss, overloaded C P U on the peer, or asymmetric routing preventing Keepalive delivery. Use the hold-time behavior to reason about how quickly a session will fail and what transient conditions are likely suspects.

Notification messages are the protocol's way of saying a fatal error has occurred and the session cannot continue. They carry an error code and subcode that indicate the reason for termination — for example, an incorrect AS in the Open, an invalid Update, or a hold timer expiration. When a Notification is received, the affected session is immediately torn down. This is deliberate: continuing after a protocol-level error could lead to incorrect routing information being accepted. A typical example from the chapter is an AS mismatch during Open; the receiver sends a Notification and both peers reset the session. It is a common mistake to treat Notification as a transient log message. In practice, receipt of a Notification requires corrective action: review the error code, fix the configuration or software bug, and then reestablish the session. When troubleshooting, capture the Notification information where available; this will point directly to the offending field — whether a mismatched AS, malformed Update, or expired timer — and avoids blind guessing. The closing lesson: Notifications stop the session to protect routing correctness, and they should guide immediate corrective steps.

The BGP Finite State Machine organizes the steps for establishing and maintaining a peering session. It defines six neighbor states: Idle, Connect, Active, OpenSent, OpenConfirm, and Established. Idle is the starting point where the process is not attempting to form a session. When the speaker initiates a TCP connection the FSM moves to Connect; a succeeding TCP handshake sends the FSM to OpenSent, where the local side has sent an Open and awaits the peer's Open. If the TCP connection cannot be created, the FSM moves to Active and keeps trying — a signal that TCP connectivity or routing to the peer is failing. Upon receiving a peer Open, a speaker enters OpenConfirm and exchanges Keepalive to confirm the parameters. Finally, after successful Keepalive exchange the session reaches Established and Update messages flow. Transitions are driven by concrete events: successful TCP connection, receipt of specific messages, or timeouts. A practical misconception is to treat Active as a BGP problem; it almost always points to TCP connectivity issues like blocked port 179, incorrect peer IP, or routing problems. Understanding this sequence allows you to map observed state to a short list of focused checks and avoid wasted effort on irrelevant settings.

Idle is the entry state for BGP. A speaker in Idle is not attempting to form a session; it may be administratively disabled or waiting for a start event. If you see Idle persistently, first check whether the BGP process or the neighbor statement is active. Moving from Idle to Connect happens when the speaker initiates a TCP connection to its peer. Connect indicates the system has started active connection attempts. If the TCP handshake succeeds the state moves to OpenSent. If the TCP handshake fails, the FSM moves to Active and repeatedly attempts a connection.
